title: Limerick and the broken treatystone
html_source:
The Treaty of Limerick (in Irish, Conradh Luimnigh) ended the Williamite War in Ireland (1688-1691) and was reputedly signed on a large block of limestone called the Treaty Stone. To this day, the stone is displayed on a large pedestal in Limerick. It remains intact, so references to breaking it here must be figurative: several articles in the treaty protecting the rights of Jacobites and Catholic gentry were ultimately not honored.

After the Jacobites (supporters of the deposed King James II) lost the Battle of the Boyne (1690), William issued the Declaration of Finglas which pardoned Jacobite soldiers but not senior officers. The officers kept fighting and saw a major victory in the Siege of Limerick (1691). However, in the next year they suffered decisive losses at the hands of the Williamites at the Battle of Aughrim and the Second Siege of Limerick.
